rationale: I'm replacing the Fisher-z Pearson features with a tangent-space embedding of Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage covariances on CC200. This approach was the most reliable connectome pipeline in large rs-fMRI benchmarks (Dadi et al. 2019). It respects the geometry of covariance matrices and lowers between-subject variance. The shrinkage also keeps short scans (some sites have fewer timepoints than ROIs) and all-zero ROIs well-conditioned. The reference mean comes only from the training fold, and the classifier is unchanged.

ADHD-200 has large site differences, and they dominate the shared tangent-space reference. I'll whiten each subject's covariance by the Riemannian mean of its own site (Riemannian Procrustes/re-centering), so the classifier learns differences within each site. To keep the useful information that ADHD rates differ by site, I'll add a smoothed site log-odds prior from the training fold back onto the decision score.

Sex is a strong, well-documented ADHD covariate in ADHD-200, since most ADHD cases are boys, and age also matters. But one sex column appended to about 20k heavily regularized connectome features would get almost no weight. So I'll stack instead: grouped inner CV (using `ctx["groups_train"]`) produces out-of-fold scores from the tangent-space logistic regression, and a small second-stage logistic regression combines those scores with sex and age.

rationale: Last round's stacking idea (adding sex and age, which are strong ADHD-200 covariates, on top of the connectome score) probably failed because it refit the slow Riemannian tangent-space step inside every inner fold. This version fits the tangent space and scaler once per training fold; that is label-free, so it doesn't leak. Grouped inner CV then reruns only the cheap logistic regression to get out-of-fold connectome scores, and a small second-stage logistic regression combines those scores with sex and standardized age.

ADHD prevalence differs a lot between ADHD-200 sites (some sites are nearly all controls). The harness groups by subject, so test-fold sites also appear in training, and the site base rate is real covariate information that sex and age don't capture. I'm adding one-hot site indicators to the second-stage stacker, next to the connectome score, sex and age. This uses the site information without the per-site re-centering that broke round 2. Sites missing from the training fold get all-zero indicators.

Different parcellations capture partly independent connectivity information, and multi-atlas ensembles have been a consistent win on ADHD-200 and ABIDE. This change adds two more connectome scores to the existing stacker, alongside CC200. They come from the anatomical AAL and Harvard-Oxford (HO) atlases and use the same tangent-space LW + L2 logistic regression pipeline. Each atlas gets its own out-of-fold score from grouped inner CV, and the second-stage logistic regression learns how to weight them next to sex, age and site.

The connectome scores are built from correlation matrices, so they ignore each ROI's signal amplitude. Altered low-frequency fluctuation amplitude (ALFF) in ADHD is well documented (Zang et al. 2007). This change adds one more stacked score from each subject's per-ROI log standard deviation across all three atlases, an ALFF-like measure. The profile is centred within each subject so scanner and site gain cancels, and dead ROIs are imputed. The stacker weights this score next to the connectome scores, sex, age and site.

Site effects are the largest source of variance in ADHD-200 tangent-space connectomes. In this version each atlas's tangent features are mean-centred within each site, with site means from the training fold only and shrunk toward the global mean for small sites. The centred features from all atlases are concatenated and fed to one extra L2 logistic regression score. This is added to the stacker next to the existing uncentred scores, and the site one-hot indicators still carry the site base rates. Round 2 failed because it replaced the original features outright; here the raw scores stay, so the stacker can ignore the new score if site removal hurts.

ADHD-200 sites recruited differently: in some, controls are sex-balanced while ADHD cases are mostly boys, and age ranges differ by group. Sex and age therefore predict diagnosis differently at each site. I'm adding site×sex and site×age interaction terms (one-hot site times standardized covariate) to the second-stage stacker so it can learn these site-specific recruitment effects instead of one pooled slope.

I'm adding one more low-dimensional score to the stacker, built from each ROI's connectivity strength (its mean Fisher-z correlation to all other ROIs) across all three atlases. Altered hub strength in default-mode and fronto-striatal regions is a reported ADHD finding, and a profile of about 430 features should be steadier than about 20k tangent edges. To remove site and scan-length effects (Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage scales all off-diagonal values by an amount that depends on the number of timepoints), I z-score each subject's profile across ROIs, which removes both the overall level and the scale.

I'm adding one more stacked score built from each ROI's intrinsic neural timescale: lag-1 autocorrelation of the ROI time series, Fisher-z transformed and centred within each subject across all three atlases. Altered intrinsic timescales have been reported in ADHD and autism, and this temporal-memory information is not captured by the amplitude or connectivity scores. Centring within subject removes the global shift caused by site TR and filtering.

Use inner grouped CV on the training fold to pick the L2 strength of each base logistic regression, instead of fixing it at C=0.001 for tangent features and C=0.01 for amplitude. The blocks differ a lot in size (AAL has about 6.8k tangent features, CC200 about 20k, amplitude about 430), so each probably needs a different amount of regularization. The candidate values are compared using out-of-fold predictions the stacker already computes, so this adds little run time.
